options: A separate Azure subscription dedicated to storage
A virtual machine's attached data disk
A type of Azure Policy rule
The namespace inside a storage account where blobs actually live, Azure's equivalent of an S3 bucket
questions.explain: A container is where blobs are organized inside a storage account — the same object-storage idea as an S3 bucket, with Azure's name attached.

questions.q: Which access tier has the lowest storage cost but requires an hours-long rehydration before you can read the data?
options: Premium
Archive
Hot
Cool
questions.explain: Archive is the cheapest storage tier, but the data is offline and must be rehydrated (which can take hours) before it can be accessed.

questions.q: Which tier fits data you read or write frequently, with no retrieval delay?
options: Archive
Hot
Cold
Cool
questions.explain: Hot has the highest storage cost but the lowest (effectively no) access cost or delay, matching frequently accessed data.

questions.q: In the nightly-backup scenario, why move backups to Cool after 7 days instead of leaving them in Hot?
options: Azure requires blobs to change tiers every 7 days
Hot tier automatically deletes blobs after 7 days
They're unlikely to be restored that soon, so paying Hot prices stops making sense while still needing fast-enough access
Cool tier blobs can no longer be restored at all
questions.explain: Cool keeps retrieval fast while cutting storage cost — the right fit once a backup is past the window where it's likely to be restored immediately.

questions.q: What does the --tier flag do on an az storage blob upload command?
options: Has no effect; tiers can only be set in the portal
Encrypts the blob with a customer-managed key
Sets the access tier (e.g. Cool) the uploaded blob is stored at
Sets the performance tier of the entire storage account
questions.explain: --tier on az storage blob upload assigns that specific blob's access tier (Hot, Cool, or Archive) at upload time.
